section: Germany and Switzerland: frontier commuters, weekly stayers and movers, tax year 2026
wording: This skill works out which country taxes the pay of a person who lives on one side of the German-Swiss border and works on the other, and how Germany taxes the result. It also lists the German rules that follow a German who moves to Switzerland. It works from the treaty of 11 August 1971 as amended by the protocol of 21 August 2023. That protocol came into force on 27 November 2025 and applies from 1 January 2026.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **1. Frontier commuter (Grenzgänger), art. 15a.** A person resident in one state whose place of work is in the other state and who regularly returns from there to their home. The pay is taxed in the state of residence. The work state may withhold tax, capped at 4.5% of gross pay if the person shows an official residence certificate from their home tax office (art. 15a(1)).
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Place of work** is normally where the employee is integrated into the employer's business. For drivers and field staff, days away count as business trips when counting non-return days. Where the contract names several sites or none, the place of work is where the work is mostly done (protocol no. 5(a)).
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Regular return, new from 2026.** There is a regular return only if the employee travels from home to the place of work and back on at least 20% of the agreed working days in the calendar year (protocol no. 5(b)). Agreed working days are those in the contract. Protocol no. 5(d) takes leave and sick days out of the working days for the 60-day test; the protocol does not say whether they also come out of the base for the 20% test, so check both bases (Example 2 passes and fails the same way on either).
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **The 60 non-return days test.** A person who does not return home after every working day keeps commuter status unless, when employed for the whole calendar year, they fail to return home on more than 60 working days because of their work (art. 15a(2)).
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **What counts as a non-return day.** A day on which returning home was not possible or not reasonable for work reasons, and the person in fact did not return. Return is not reasonable when the shortest road distance one way is over 100 km by car, or the fastest public transport one way at usual commuting times takes over 1.5 hours; the means of transport mostly used decides (protocol no. 5(e), which takes over the consultation agreement of 12 October 2018). One-day business trips in either treaty state are not non-return days; one-day trips to a third country always are (protocol no. 5(f)). Weekend and holiday days on a multi-day business trip paid by the employer, and days off worked on the employer's express order, are working days (protocol no. 5(d)). Shift work spread over several days does not break the regular return; breaks under four hours do not end the working day (protocol no. 5(c)).
disposition: Exact prior current unit with rebound native coordinates

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Home office days.** Under the consultation agreement of 15 and 18 July 2022 (BMF letter of 26 July 2022), a working day spent entirely at home in the residence state is not a non-return day. That agreement was made under the treaty as amended in 2010; whether it still applies under the 2026 protocol is not confirmed (see the end of this skill). Either way, a home office day is not a day on which the person travels to the place of work and back, so from 2026 it counts against the 20% regular-return test.

section: Who this applies to
wording: The rule works both ways. For a Swiss resident who commutes to a German employer, the German employer withholds at most 4.5% and Switzerland taxes the pay, cutting the gross pay by one fifth when computing its tax base (art. 15a(3)(b)).

section: Who this applies to
wording: **2. Weekly stayer (Wochenaufenthalter) and others who lose commuter status.** After actual commuter status fails, test art. 15(2) before allocating Swiss work pay under art. 15(1): pay remains taxable only in the residence state if presence in the other state is not more than 183 days in the relevant calendar year, the actual treaty employer is not resident there, and its permanent establishment there does not bear the remuneration. Count presence days, not just working days; establish employer and any economic-employer issue from the actual facts. An ordinary German-resident non-commuter present for 80 days in Switzerland for an actual German treaty employer, with no Swiss permanent establishment bearing the pay and all other stated gates met, stays exclusively German-taxable on that pay. At 184 days or with a Swiss-resident employer, that exception fails; then art. 15(1), subject to the other actual special rules, allows Swiss taxation of pay for work there. Germany exempts qualifying pay with progression (art. 24(1) no. 1(c), no. 2; § 32b(1) no. 3 EStG), only on proof either that Switzerland waived its taxing right or that Swiss tax assessed on the pay was paid (§ 50d(8)); a bare zero-withholding certificate does not itself establish a waiver. Under that ordinary art. 15(1) workday route, pay for days outside Switzerland stays German-taxable. Existing examples with a Swiss employer do not meet art. 15(2)(b).

section: Who this applies to
wording: A weekday flat does not by itself move the person's residence. If the person is resident in both states under domestic law, art. 4(2) decides: permanent home first, then centre of vital interests (closer personal and economic ties), then habitual abode, then nationality. A family home in Germany usually points to Germany.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **3. Managers of Swiss companies, art. 15(4).** A German resident who is a board member (Vorstandsmitglied), director, managing director (Geschäftsführer) or Prokurist of a Swiss company can be taxed in Switzerland on that pay, unless their duties are limited to work outside Switzerland. Art. 15a takes priority, so a manager who meets the commuter test is a commuter. The German and Swiss authorities agreed on 6 April 2023 to apply art. 15(4) also to people registered with a signature right and no stated function, and to unregistered people with powers at least equal to a Prokura. That agreement now runs to 31 December 2027 (BMF letters of 25 April 2023 and 16 October 2025).

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Treaty tail, art. 4(4).** A Swiss resident without Swiss nationality who was fully taxable in Germany for at least five years in total remains taxable in Germany on German-source income in the year their German liability ended and the five following years. The separate art. 4(4) credit, under the actual German foreign-tax-credit rules and excluding trade tax, covers treaty-permitted Swiss tax only against the additional German tax imposed by this tail beyond what arts. 6–22 otherwise permit. Stipulated German tail tax EUR 300, otherwise treaty-permitted German tax EUR 100 and otherwise eligible Swiss tax EUR 250 give an additional-tax cap of EUR 200, credit EUR 200 and German remainder EUR 100. These are independently established inputs, not an official example or the full commuter § 36 settlement credit. This does not apply to someone who moved to take up genuine employment with an employer in which they have no substantial interest. A German employer may not apply the 4.5% cap to such a person while art. 4(4) applies (Gre-1 note 3).
disposition: R47–54 bounded source-backed condition successor

section: Who this applies to
wording: **Lump-sum taxpayers, art. 4(6).** A person is not treated as resident in a treaty state if that state does not tax them, at the generally applied taxes, on all their income from the other state that is normally taxable there. A lump-sum (expenditure-based) taxpayer in Switzerland who is not taxed on German-source income at ordinary rates therefore loses treaty protection. The Swiss rules on the lump sum are in ch-cross-border.

section: Step 2: the German assessment of a commuter (German resident)
wording: - The 2026 tariff applies to taxable income. For ordinary assessment without a separate § 32d(3)/(4) component, establish the actual Soli base and threshold: EUR 20,350 for a single assessment, EUR 40,700 for the statutory joint cases. Up to that threshold the ordinary surcharge is zero; above it take the smaller of 5.5% of the base and 11.9% of its excess over that threshold, dropping fractions of a cent. A stipulated ordinary single base of EUR 20,400 gives min(EUR 1,122, EUR 5.95) = EUR 5.95. Use the employee companion for child-related base and special § 32d selectors; Swiss § 36 withholding credit is a settlement credit, not a reduction of this Soli assessment base.

section: Step 4: Swiss occupational pensions of former commuters
wording: Protocol no. 9 covers Swiss second-pillar insurance payments where the last or current employment relevant to that insurance relationship before payment/start was in Swiss public service, including the specified vested-benefit accounts/policies. For a recipient who has or had art. 15a commuter status, art. 19(4) gives residence-state priority and the other state limits withholding under art. 15a. For recurring payments, give the second-pillar institution the prescribed residence certificate before the first receipt (Gre-4, or Gre-5 for survivors); capital payments instead require commuter-status certification in the prescribed official refund form. Merely having worked in Swiss public service sometime is insufficient. German credit of Swiss withholding requires the corresponding receipts actually to enter the German tax base and no refund to have been applied for or made. Preserve the actual pension classification/taxable-share limit: the cited 2018 method credits at most the corresponding 4.5% share for the Obligatorium or the relevant Ertragsanteil for the Überobligatorium; no universal pension percentage or double recovery is inferred.

section: Example 2: part-time commuter with home office and overnight trips
wording: Jonas lives in Konstanz and works three days a week for a Zurich employer all of 2026. His contract does not state the usual full-time days, so a five-day week gives 240. His contractual days are 3/5 of 240 = 144. He takes 12 days of leave, so he has 132 working days. He works 30 of them at home in Konstanz and stays overnight in Switzerland on 30 days because of evening client work more than 100 km from home. (Invented case.)

section: Example 2: part-time commuter with home office and overnight trips
wording: - Non-return limit: 60 × 144 / 240 = 36 days (leave is not deducted for this ratio). His 30 days are within it.

section: Example 2: part-time commuter with home office and overnight trips
wording: - Regular return: commuting days = 132 − 30 − 30 = 72. 20% of 132 = 26.4. 72 is above, so he passes. On the contract days without deducting leave (144) the threshold is 28.8; he still passes.

section: Example 2: part-time commuter with home office and overnight trips
wording: - Edge case: if he had worked 80 days at home, his commuting days would be 132 − 80 − 30 = 22, below 26.4 (and below 28.8). He would then fail the regular-return test from 2026 even though the home office days are not non-return days. Art. 15 would then apply: Switzerland taxes pay for his Swiss work days and Germany exempts it with progression, on proof of Swiss tax.
